title: Facilitate a group to achieve a stated objective or solve a problem

lessons.title: The role of a facilitator
lessons.html:
Facilitating is not lecturing

A facilitator helps a group to think, discuss and decide for itself. The facilitator manages the process, while the group owns the content and the decisions. This is different from a trainer who transfers knowledge, or a chairperson who leads with authority. In extension, you will facilitate farmer associations, cooperatives, dip tank committees, study groups and project steering committees.

Qualities of a good facilitator

  • Neutral: does not push personal views or take sides in disputes.
  • Good listener: listens actively, summarises and checks understanding.
  • Inclusive: makes sure quiet members, women, youth and newcomers are heard.
  • Organised: prepares well, keeps time and records outcomes.
  • Respectful: respects local culture, language and leadership structures.

Preparing to facilitate

  1. Agree with the group leaders on the objective of the session, stated clearly. For example: agree on a fair schedule for using the shared irrigation pump.
  2. Find out who will attend, existing tensions and the relevant background.
  3. Plan an agenda with time for each item and choose suitable methods.
  4. Arrange a venue that is accessible, comfortable and neutral, with materials such as flip charts and markers.
  5. Decide on the language of the meeting and arrange interpretation if needed.

Group development

Groups often go through stages: forming, when members are polite and unsure; storming, when disagreements surface; norming, when they agree on ways of working; and performing, when they work well together. Conflict in the storming stage is normal. A facilitator helps the group move through it rather than avoiding it.

Ground rules

At the start, ask the group to agree on rules such as: one person speaks at a time, respect all views, phones on silent, and decisions are made by agreed methods. Write them on a flip chart and refer back to them when needed.

lessons.title: Methods for problem solving and decision making
lessons.html:
A structured problem-solving process

Groups make better decisions when they follow clear steps.

  1. Define the problem: agree on exactly what the problem is. Example: three of the eight members get most of the pump time, and others' vegetables are wilting.
  2. Analyse causes: ask why the problem happens. Use a problem tree or ask why repeatedly until root causes appear, such as no written schedule and no record of fuel contributions.
  3. Generate options: use brainstorming. All ideas are written down without criticism at first.
  4. Evaluate options: compare options against criteria such as cost, fairness, practicality and acceptance by members.
  5. Decide: choose an option using the agreed method.
  6. Plan action: who will do what by when.
  7. Review: meet again to check whether the solution works.

Useful participatory tools

  • Brainstorming for many ideas quickly.
  • Small group work so that more people can contribute.
  • Ranking or voting with stones or beans, useful where literacy is low.
  • Seasonal calendars to plan work around rainfall and labour peaks.
  • Resource maps drawn on the ground or paper to discuss grazing, water and fields.

Ways of deciding

MethodWhen useful
ConsensusImportant decisions that need everyone's support
Majority voteWhen consensus cannot be reached and the constitution allows it
DelegationTechnical matters given to a committee or expert

Agree on the decision method before discussing the options, so nobody feels the rules changed afterwards. Check the group's constitution for formal decisions such as electing office bearers or spending funds.

lessons.title: Handling difficult dynamics and closing well
lessons.html:
Managing group dynamics

Every group has members who behave in ways that can block progress. A skilled facilitator handles these situations calmly and respectfully.

BehaviourFacilitator response
One person dominatesThank them, then invite others by name or use a round where everyone speaks briefly
Silent membersUse small groups or pairs, ask for their experience directly but gently
Side conversationsRefer to the ground rules, ask if the point should be shared with all
Going off topicWrite the issue on a parking-lot sheet for later, return to the agenda
Heated conflictPause, restate the shared objective, let each side explain without interruption, focus on interests not personalities

Conflict as opportunity

Disagreement often shows that people care. Help the group separate the people from the problem. Ask each side what they need, not only what they want. For instance, one member wants more pump time; the underlying need may be water for a crop already contracted to a buyer. Understanding needs often reveals solutions acceptable to all.

If a conflict involves threats or violence, stop the meeting, ensure everyone's safety and involve the leaders or authorities. Never put yourself or participants in danger.

Closing the session

  • Summarise the decisions and the action plan.
  • Confirm who does what and by when.
  • Agree on the date of the follow-up meeting.
  • Ask for quick feedback on the session.
  • Thank participants.

Afterwards, send or present the minutes or notes, including the action list. Follow up on actions before the next meeting. The group's trust grows when it sees that decisions lead to real results.

Key points

  • The facilitator manages the process; the group owns decisions.
  • Prepare a clear objective, agenda and ground rules.
  • Use a structured problem-solving process and participatory tools.
  • Agree on the decision method before discussing options.
  • Handle dominance, silence and conflict respectfully and close with a clear action plan.
